problem: Visual navigation models for urban sidewalks are only evaluated in small, short-horizon (about 10 m), low-diversity scenarios with no standardized protocol and no isolation of pedestrian behaviors. Existing social-navigation benchmarks are indoor, and outdoor 3DGS benchmarks lack dynamic pedestrians.
motivation: Sidewalk robots (delivery robots, wheelchairs) must handle long routes, varied structures and reactive pedestrians. Without a unified benchmark, models cannot be compared fairly and bottlenecks cannot be identified. A scalable, reproducible simulator with controllable pedestrian events would expose failure modes and could also generate training data.
key_idea: Build an Isaac Sim benchmark of procedurally generated and real-scanned (3DGS) sidewalk scenes with event-triggered, SMPL-based pedestrian behaviors, and evaluate 9 visual navigation models on unit-test, pedestrian-reactive and long-horizon scenarios.
insight: Sidewalk-specific data scale matters most: OpenPilot (1000 h, tiny 8M regression model) beats larger or architecturally fancier models, and general models like ViNT/NoMaD get about 0 SR. Pedestrian behaviors, especially gestures and crosswalk crossing, remain near-unsolved (Ped-Crossing avg 0.01 SR). The VLA InternVLA-N1 has poor control but the best pedestrian distance and collision rate, suggesting a combination of VLA reasoning with low-level policies. Fine-tuning FlowPilot on 500 synthetic demos raises Ped-Crossing sim from 0.11 to 0.69, showing simulation as a data source.
method: Procedural scenes: 7 primitive block types joined by spline routing, split into 5 functional zones, filled with UrbanVerse-100K assets; 100 environments of 2 km x 2 km.

Real-scanned scenes: XGRIDS LiDAR+4-camera scans reconstructed as 3DGS for appearance and a mesh for geometry/physics, with sidewalk and crosswalk regions annotated; 11 scenes averaging 150 m x 150 m.

Event-based pedestrian behaviors: behavior graphs plus a state machine, with 8 behaviors (Obstructing, Conversing, Queueing, Frontal, Lateral, Overtaking, Ped-Crossing, Gesturing) triggered by relative robot position, using hand-crafted trajectories and speeds; ORCA and Push-and-Rotate for regular walking.

SMPL-based pedestrian animation: SMPL parameters driven by MotionLCM and Motion-X retrieval, rendered as textured meshes or human 3DGS avatars with a custom Nvdiffrast renderer composited over the simulator background; 60x faster than the Isaac Sim native module (226.8 FPS vs 3.4 FPS with 50 pedestrians).

Three scenario suites: 330 unit-tests (straight/curve/crosswalk, 10-20 m, 60 s limit), 800 pedestrian-reactive (100 per behavior, procedural only), 105 long-horizon (>100 m, 36.5 km total, reset to nearest waypoint on failure and count failures).

Evaluation protocol: synchronized stepping, a shared PD controller converting waypoints to velocities, a four-wheeled delivery robot, and goals with no privileged leakage (random intermediate point goals, random images for image-goal models, 'Follow the sidewalk' for InternVLA-N1). Metrics are route completion, SR, SPL, failures per 100 m, and velocity.
Synthetic-data fine-tuning: 500 ORCA-generated demos per scenario, fine-tuning only the action encoder/decoder of FlowPilot.

setting.backbone: 9 evaluated models: ViNT, NoMaD, MBRA, InternVLA-N1 (7B VLM), MIMIC, S2E, CityWalker, FlowPilot, OpenPilot (pretrained, evaluated as is; FlowPilot fine-tuned in one experiment)
setting.training_data: Benchmark paper; evaluated models use general data or 50-1000 h of sidewalk data. Fine-tuning uses 500 synthetic demos per scenario for FlowPilot.
setting.observation: monocular RGB (resolution and FPS matched to each model), plus goal input per model (point, image, language or none)
setting.action_space: predicted waypoints converted by a PD controller to linear and angular velocity (max 2.5 m/s, 0.65 rad/s)
setting.simulator: NVIDIA Isaac Sim 6.0 / Isaac Lab (procedural scenes and 3DGS real scans)
setting.privileged: none for the evaluated models (goals sampled to avoid leaking routes); the ORCA planner is used only to generate fine-tuning demonstrations

numbers.extra: Procedurally generated scenes, straight blocks; RC = route completion
Success rate per behavior; Static reference 0.78; Ped-Crossing 0.00
Failures per 100 m: FC total, C collision, OL out-of-lane, F freezing; V is velocity in m/s

numbers_note: Fig. 2 (unit-test RC) and the Fig. long-horizon plots are given as figures, with the full values in appendix tables. All entries are benchmark results for existing models, not a proposed model. The split is set to 'test' because the benchmark has no official train/val split.
results: Sidewalk-specific data scale dominates. OpenPilot (1000 h) is best overall, with 0.78/0.57/0.98 SR on procedural straight/curve/crosswalk unit tests and 1.34 failures per 100 m in long-horizon runs. General models (ViNT, NoMaD) get about 0 SR. Pedestrian behaviors are hard (avg SR from 0.42 static to 0.23 obstructing, 0.01 Ped-Crossing, 0.05 Gesturing), and OpenPilot at 2 km would still need about 26.6 takeovers. Synthetic fine-tuning lifts FlowPilot Ped-Crossing from 0.11 to 0.69 in sim and 0.00 to 0.40 in the real world.
limitations: Pedestrian behaviors are rule-based with hand-crafted trajectories, which may lack real-world realism; the pedestrian renderer trades visual quality for speed, widening the real-to-sim gap.
Only 11 real-scanned scenes (5 long-horizon), with pedestrians only in procedural scenes; synchronized testing ignores inference latency, and simulated terrain is mostly flat.
The synthetic fine-tuning experiment is preliminary (one model, two scenarios, 10 real trials).
